title: str.title() turns "mcdonald" into "Mcdonald" and "they're" into "They'Re"
assumption: A built-in title-case function always produces the conventionally correct capitalization of a name.

input.description: A lowercase or all-caps name from a legacy database or a careless import, being 'fixed up' for display with a generic title-casing function.

what_goes_wrong: "mcdonald" displays as "Mcdonald" instead of "McDonald", and a word containing an apostrophe like "they're" gets a capital letter injected right after the apostrophe, becoming "They'Re".
why: Python's str.title() capitalizes the first letter of every maximal run of alphabetic characters and lowercases the rest; it has no dictionary of surname conventions, so it has no way to know the 'D' in McDonald should also be capitalized, and it treats an apostrophe as a word boundary just like a space — which happens to look right for a name like "o'neil" but is wrong for a contraction like "they're", capitalizing the letter right after the apostrophe either way. The common hand-rolled JavaScript equivalent (capitalize the first character of each whitespace-separated token) fails differently: it also gives "Mcdonald", but treats "o'neil" as one token and returns "O'neil", missing the capital that name needs.
fix: Don't auto-capitalize a name with a generic title-casing function; either store and display the name exactly as the person entered it, or maintain an explicit exception list for known patterns (Mc/Mac, O', particles) and accept that no automatic rule covers every name.

sources.title: Patrick McKenzie: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names

test_cases.note: A generic title-case function will almost certainly fail this — decide whether you want to auto-capitalize names at all before relying on one.
